links.comparator_used: Student-authored human-only note without AI input, compared with a hybrid note revised after reviewing an AI scribe draft (paired, same students, OSCE)
links.outcome: QNOTE element scores (0-100) rated by blinded raters across 10 note elements
links.effect: Little change across elements. The only notable shift was a chief complaint decline (median 50 vs 50, mean 69.1 vs 59.6, P=.05), with fewer fully acceptable (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more unacceptable (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%) hybrid notes. All other elements were similar (P=.14-.97). Of 12 students in the bottom quartile of human-only scores, 9 (75%) improved; 5/47 (10.6%) declined by 20 points or more.
links.tradeoff: AI notes often omitted symptom duration (mentioned in the chief complaint of only 8/47, 17%). 26/47 (55.3%) agreed the AI note left out important details, and 10/47 (21.3%) agreed it may reduce their ability to learn note writing. Students wrote their own note first (cognitive forcing), so the AI was not a true first draft. The study was nonrandomized, with self-selected participants, preclerkship students and a single site.
links.quote: After writing high-quality “human-only” notes, interaction with notes generated by the AI scribe had little impact on the quality of the “hybrid” notes written by preclerkship medical students.

design_hint: requiring independent human note before AI-note review (human-in-the-loop hybrid editing)
